steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Cholesterol Levels: What You Need to Know.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Monitor eGFR and serum potassium within 1–2 weeks of initiating or titrating RAAS inhibitors.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use statins with caution in active hepatic disease; monitor baseline ALT/AST.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and statins are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).
special_populations.elderly: Avoid overtreatment; monitor for orthostatic hypotension and fall risk.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is cholesterol? Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some cholesterol to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases . How do you measure cholesterol levels? A blood test called a lipoprotein or lipid panel can measure your cholesterol levels. Before the test, you'll usually need to fast (not eat or drink anything but water) for 9 to 12 hours. Follow the instructions your health care provider gives you. The test gives information about your: Total cholesterol. This is a measure of the total amount of cholesterol in your blood. It includes both low-density lipoprotein ( LDL ) cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein ( HDL ) cholesterol. LDL cholesterol. LDL is often called "bad" cholesterol because it is the main source of cholesterol buildup and blockage in the arteries. HDL cholesterol. HDL is often called "good" cholesterol because it helps remove cholesterol from your arteries. Non-HDL. This number is your total cholesterol minus your HDL. Your non-HDL includes LDL and other types of cholesterol such as VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein). It gives a better picture of all the "bad" types of cholesterol that can raise your heart risk. Triglycerides . This is another type of fat in your blood that can raise your risk of heart disease, especially in women . What do my cholesterol numbers mean? Cholesterol numbers are measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Talk with your provider about what your cholesterol numbers should be. The numbers that are best for you may depend on your age, race, blood pressure, weight, family history, and more. However, here are some general guidelines showing the desirable levels (levels that are healthy for most people): Anyone age 19 or younger: Type of Cholesterol Healthy Level Total Cholesterol Less than 170 mg/dL Non-HDL Less than 120 mg/dL LDL Less than 110 mg/dL HDL More than 45mg/dL Men age 20 or older: Type of Cholesterol Healthy Level Total Cholesterol Less than 200 mg/dL Non-HDL Less than 130 mg/dL LDL Less than 100 mg/dL HDL Greater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best. Levels less than 40 mg/dL are considered low. Women age 20 or older: Type of Cholesterol Healthy Level Total Cholesterol Less than 200 mg/dL Non-HDL Less than 130 mg/dL LDL Less than 100 mg/dL HDL Greater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best. Levels less than 50 mg/dL are considered low. Triglycerides are not a type of cholesterol, but they are also measured in this test. A normal triglyceride level is below 150 mg/dL. You might need treatment if you have triglyceride levels that are borderline high (150-199 mg/dL) or high (200 mg/dL or more). What are risk-based LDL goals? If you have heart disease, or your provider thinks you might be at higher risk, they may use your LDL cholesterol level to help you set goals for your LDL cholesterol levels. Your provider may use a new risk estimator tool called PREVENT, which stands for Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs, to guide these goals and estimate your risk of heart disease. It looks at factors like your age, health history, and family history, and puts you in a risk group. LDL goal by risk level Risk level Healthy LDL Level Low or borderline risk 100 mg/dL or below High risk of future heart attack or stroke 70 mg/dL or below Already have heart disease 70 mg/dL or below Already have heart disease and are at very high risk 55 mg/dL or below How often should I get a cholesterol test? When and how often you should get a cholesterol test depends on your age, risk factors, and family history. The general recommendations are: For people who are age 21 or younger: Children should be screened at least once between ages 9 to 11 and again once between ages 17 and 21 Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family history of high cholesterol, heart attack , or stroke For people who are ages 21 to 65: Younger adults should have the test every 5 years Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years For people older than 65: They should be tested every year Additional testing may include: A lipoprotein(a) blood test once as an adult, and an apolipoprotein B or "apo B" test if you have certain health conditions. These special blood tests help your provider understand your heart risk. A coronary calcium scan may be done to help determine if you need cholesterol medicines. This is an imaging test which checks to see if you have calcium built up in your heart arteries. What affects my cholesterol levels? Many factors can affect your cholesterol levels. Some of them are things you can change: Diet. Saturated fat and cholesterol in the food you eat make your blood cholesterol level rise. Saturated fat is the main problem, but cholesterol in foods also matters. Reducing the amount of saturated fat in your diet helps lower your blood cholesterol level. Foods that have high levels of saturated fats include red meats, full-fat dairy products, chocolate, some baked goods, and many deep-fried and processed foods. Weight. Being overweight or having obesity are risk factors for heart disease. They also tend to increase your cholesterol. If you have high cholesterol and are overweight, it's recommended that you lose at least 5% of your body weight, which would be 10 pounds for a 200-pound person. Lack of physical activity . Not being physically active is a risk factor for heart disease. Smoking. Cigarette smoking lowers your HDL cholesterol. Since HDL helps to remove cholesterol from your arteries, having a lower HDL level can contribute to a higher cholesterol level. Some factors that you cannot change can also affect your cholesterol levels, such as Age. Your cholesterol levels tend to rise as you get older. Even though it is less common, younger people, including children and teens , can also have high cholesterol. Sex. Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of high total cholesterol than women. But after menopause , a woman's risk goes up. This happens because menopause lowers levels of female hormones that may protect against high blood cholesterol. Family history. Your genes partly determine how much cholesterol your body makes. High cholesterol can run in families. Ethnicity. Your ethnicity may increase your risk of high cholesterol. How can I lower my cholesterol? You can lower your cholesterol through heart-healthy lifestyle changes: They include a heart-healthy eating plan , weight management , and regular physical activity . If the lifestyle changes alone do not lower your cholesterol enough, you may also need to take medicines. There are several types of cholesterol-lowering drugs available, including statins . You may need a statin if you: Are age 30 or older and have an LDL cholesterol of 160 mg/dL or higher Have a strong family history of heart disease If you take medicines to lower your cholesterol, you still should continue with the lifestyle changes. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
style_3_monograph.treatment: Steps you can take to improve your cholesterol levels and to help prevent heart disease and a heart attack include: Quit smoking . This is the single biggest change you can make to reduce your risk of heart attack and stroke. Eat a heart-healthy diet . This includes foods that are naturally low in fat such as vegetables, fruits and whole-grains. Use low-fat toppings, sauces, and dressings. Avoid foods that are high in saturated fat . Exercise regularly. Lose weight if you are overweight or have obesity. Your provider may want you to take medicine for your cholesterol if lifestyle changes do not work. This will depend on: Your age Whether or not you have heart disease, diabetes, or other blood vessel problems Whether you smoke or are overweight Whether you have high blood pressure or diabetes You are more likely to need medicine to lower your cholesterol : If you have heart disease or diabetes If you are at high risk for heart disease (even if you do not yet have any heart problems) If your LDL cholesterol is 160 mg/dL (4.14 mmol/L) or higher Your lipoprotein (a) [(lp(a)] level is 125 nmol/L or 50 mg/dL or higher There are several types of medicines to help lower blood cholesterol levels. The medicines work in different ways. Statins are one kind of medicine that lowers cholesterol and has been proven to reduce the chance of heart disease. Other medicines are available if your risk is high and statins do not lower your cholesterol levels enough. These include ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and PCSK9 inhibitors. Check with your provider about what is best for you.
